subject: Critical Thinking
title: Tu Quoque: Two Wrongs Make a Right?
description: A fast breakdown of Tu Quoque: Two Wrongs Make a Right? for builders.

hook.text: 'You should stop smoking.' 'But you smoke too!' The health effects of smoking don't change based on who says it.

buildup.text: Tu quoque (you too): deflecting criticism by pointing out the critic does the same thing. Also called 'whataboutism.'

discovery.text: Soviet propaganda perfected it: any criticism of the USSR was met with 'And you're lynching Negroes' – a real Soviet.

twist.text: It's psychologically satisfying because it feels fair. But consistency of the speaker doesn't affect truth of the claim.

climax.text: Tu quoque is the internet's favorite fallacy.

punchline.text: Hypocrisy doesn't make someone wrong. It makes them a hypocrite.

quiz.question: Why is tu quoque a fallacy?
options: The speaker's hypocrisy doesn't affect the truth of their claim

details.summary: Tu quoque deflects criticism by pointing out that the critic is guilty of the same thing. It does not address whether the criticism is valid — it simply tries to discredit the critic through hypocrisy charges.
details.whyItMatters: Hypocrisy does not make a claim false. Tu quoque derails accountability by shifting focus from the argument to the arguer's consistency.
takeaways: Tu quoque is Latin for 'you too' or 'you also'
The critic's behavior is irrelevant to the argument's validity
It is one of the most common deflection tactics in personal conflicts

faq.question: Is tu quoque the same thing as whataboutism?
faq.answer: They are closely related. Both deflect criticism by pointing to someone else's behavior. Whataboutism is the geopolitical version: when Country A criticizes Country B, Country B responds with 'What about your own problems?' instead of addressing the criticism.

faq.question: Can pointing out hypocrisy ever be a legitimate argument?
faq.answer: It can question someone's credibility or sincerity but never disproves their claim. A doctor who smokes is hypocritical for advising against smoking, but the medical evidence remains valid regardless of the doctor's personal choices.
